chunks: That was narrated by Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhl, from Muhammad ibn Abi Tahir ibn Tasinim, from Ya'la al-Tanafisi, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, who said:

A man died and left two grandmothers: the mother of his mother and the mother of his father. Abu Bakr gave the share to the mother of his mother and left the other. A man from the Ansar said to him: 'You have left a woman; if the two grandmothers had died while their sons were alive, they would not have inherited anything from what you gave, yet you gave to the mother of his father.' So he gave her the share.
Muhammad ibn Tasinim said: And Abu Nu'aym told me, who said: Ibrahim ibn Ismail ibn Jamii' ibn Harithah al-Ansari narrated to us, from al-Zuhri, from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, who said:

The grandmother came to Abu Bakr and said: 'My son's son has died, so give me my right.' He said: 'I do not know anything for you in the Book of Allah, but I will ask the people.' So he asked, and al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah testified for her, saying: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) gave her one-sixth.' He asked: 'Who heard with you?' He said: 'Muhammad ibn Maslamah.' So he gave her one-sixth.

Then the mother of the mother came and said: 'My daughter's son has died, so give me my right.' He said: 'You are not the one for whom it was testified that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) gave her one-sixth. If you divide it between yourselves, you are more knowledgeable.'

key_terms.السُّدُسَ: One-sixth (the specific share given to the grandmother)

ai.seo_question: What is the inheritance share of a grandmother in Shia jurisprudence according to the narration of Abu Bakr?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the evolution of the grandmother's inheritance share (al-Jaddah) from a matter of juristic discretion (ijtihad) by Abu Bakr to a confirmed prophetic precedent (sunna) through companion testimony. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the transition from early caliphal rulings to established hadith-based jurisprudence, where the maternal and paternal grandmothers are treated as equal heirs of one-sixth when no closer ascendants exist. The narrative underscores the importance of verifying legal rulings against the Prophet's practice rather than relying solely on analogical reasoning.
